item.title: NYC Council weighs how to regulate e-bikes, e-scooters, and mopeds during marathon hearing
item.dc:creator: By Ethan Stark-Miller
item.description: The NYC Council held an hours-long hearing Wednesday in which lawmakers heard testimony from city officials and the public on nearly two dozen measures aimed at strengthening regulations around e-bikes, e-scooters, and mopeds that have exploded in popularity across the five boroughs in recent years. item.content:encoded:
The NYC Council held an hours-long hearing Wednesday in which lawmakers heard testimony from city officials and the public on nearly two dozen measures aimed at strengthening regulations around e-bikes, e-scooters, and mopeds that have exploded in popularity across the five boroughs in recent years.

The 23 bills council members are proposing take a variety of approaches toward addressing persistent safety concerns around the ridership of electric micromobility devices, which are largely used by immigrant food delivery workers. Those include taking illegal devices that are involved in many crashes off the streets, outlawing the fastest legal e-bikes, and better regulating the third-party apps that employ delivery workers. 

The suite of legislation under consideration, however, does not include a measure that would require that e-bike and e-scooter owners register and license their vehicles — a bill known as “Priscilla’s Law.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who scheduled the hearing amid a spate of e-micromobility-involved crashes over the summer, said the purpose of the proceeding was both to examine how the legislation can make riding motorized two-wheelers safer and how the city is enforcing already existing laws.

"As speaker, I believe the council has a responsibility to meticulously examine the micromobility landscape and address the major gaps in our laws that have emerged, particularly as technology and transportation habits have changed," Menin said during her opening remarks. "But we also have the responsibility to hold the administration accountable for enforcing the laws that are already on the books."

Over the course of the hearing, the council heard testimony from Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration, including top officials with the Departments of Transporation (DOT) and Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) as well as the NYPD. They also heard from safe streets advocates, those in favor of stricter regulations on all e-micromobility devices, and other members of the public.

Crashes involving e-micromobility devices

The current landscape for e-bikes and e-scooters was shaped by the state's decision to legalize them in 2020.

In doing so, Albany authorized three classes of e-bikes in the city, none of which can have motors exceeding 750 watts: Class 1 — pedal-assist e-bikes that can reach 20 miles per hour; Class 2 — throttle-assist bikes that can reach 20 mph; and Class 3 — throttle-assist e-bikes that can reach 25 mph. Legal e-scooters cannot exceed 20 mph top speeds.

However, all micromobility devices in the city must abide by a 15 mph speed limit, which was instituted by former Mayor Eric Adams last year.

The hearing comes after a few high-profile crashes involving e-micromobility devices over the summer.

Among those incidents was a crash on the Queensboro Bridge between the rider of an illegal motorized scooter and a traditional cyclist, killing them both. Another incident in Lower Manhattan saw a 17-year-old riding an illegal e-moto killed when he collided with an SUV.

"We need to integrate these devices more intentionally into our street design and our regulatory schemes if we want to avoid tragedies like the ones we saw far too many of this summer," City Council Transportation Chair Shaun Abreu said during the hearing.

Several bills in the package aim to get illegal e-bikes and e-scooters, which can far exceed the 25 mph and 20 mph legal top speeds for the respective devices, off of the streets.

Officials and advocates say that while most brick-and-morter stores in the city have ceased selling illegal devices, they end up in the five boroughs anyway via online sales. In those instances, online retailers market the devices as street legal, despite that not being the case.

During his testimony, DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn said that roughly two of the 17 e-bike-related fatalities so far this year involved illegal devices, with the cause of another three being unknown. For the 11 e-scooter involved deaths this year, Flynn said, six were on illegal devices and four were unknown.

But DOT chief of staff Madeline Labadie said the agency does not have a good sense of how many e-micromobility devices currently on city streets are legal versus illegal. She said that is due to most of the vehicles being privately owned and not licensed or registered.

"Without any license requirement, there isn't a single source of truth where they are captured in terms of the amount that are on the streets or that are sold," Labadie said.

One piece of legislation meant to rein in the illegal devices, sponsored by Abreu, would allow the owners of Class 3 e-bikes or illegal devices to trade them in for legal Class 1 or 2 bikes or obtain a voucher to buy a legal device themselves.

That measure drew pushback from Flynn, who said that while DOT supports the "bill's intent," the agency has concerns about implementing it.

"Standing up a program like this is very resource-intensive and a narrower approach that targets the most dangerous illegal devices could prove a greater impact on street safety," Flynn said.

Another bill would require the NYPD and DOT to use devices known as dynamometers, which measure e-bikes' and e-scooters' voltage and maximum assisted speed in order to ascertain whether or not the devices they seize are legal.

NYPD officials who testified at the hearing said that while the idea of using dynamometers to test devices' legality is "very interesting," they still have a lot of questions about how such a program would work in practice.

"It would be new to any major American city," said Michael Gerber, the NYPD's deputy commissioner of legal matters. "That raises a host of questions in terms of procurement and cost and operational functionality, right?"

Other bills in the package, sponsored by Council Member Crystal Hudson (D-Brooklyn), seek to ban both the sale and operation of Class 3 e-bikes. The latter bill would be phased in over a two-year period, with the city distributing warnings to those still found to be riding Class 3 e-bikes through April 1, 2029, after which point they would be hit with escalating fines.

Department of Consumer and Worker Protection Commissioner Sam Levine, during his testimony, raised concerns that outlawing the operation of Class 3 e-bikes could cause issues for immigrant delivery workers who may unwittingly continue using the devices.

"We have significant concerns of unintended consequences that will most heavily impact delivery workers," Levine said. "Many of them are immigrants with limited English proficiency and other vulnerabilities. Delivery workers could face losing their livelihoods as well as increased interactions with law enforcement at a time when many are especially fearful of such interactions."

The legislation cracking down on third-party delivery apps includes bills that would require they obtain business licenses from the city Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, retain delivery data, and verify the registration of mopeds used for deliveries.

When it comes to Priscilla’s Law, some lawmakers and groups calling for cracking down on e-micromobility devices argue it would be the only effective way to regulate them.

"Shaun you asked how to tell the difference between legal and illegal e-bikes, how about license plates for the legal ones?" Janet Schroeder, co-founder of the anti-e-bike group the NYC E Vehicle Safety Alliance, said to Abreu.

But delivery workers contend it would put the largely undocumented immigrant advocates in the crosshairs of federal immigration authorities.

Ligia Guallpa, executive director of the group the Workers Justice Project, said the package of bills does not address the "root causes" of street safety.

"It leaves out the need for safer street infrastructure, stronger worker protections, a real transition plan, and real accountability to corporations," Guallpa said.

item.title: Fresh Meadows dentist busted for defrauding Medicaid out of $300K in a false billing scheme: AG James

item.content:encoded: A Fresh Meadows dentist was arrested on Monday and charged with 40 crimes for allegedly stealing more than $300,000 from Medicaid by billing for hundreds of dental procedures he never performed while his patients suffered, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on Monday, Sept. 28. Suleman Nasimi, 46, of Hicksville, LI, was arraigned in Queens Criminal Court on Monday on two separate 40-count felony complaints following an investigation by the Office of the Attorney General’s (OAG) Medicaid Fraud Control Unit (MFCU) found that Nasimi allegedly submitted false claims to Medicaid, even billing Medicaid for procedures conducted on the same days he was on vacation in Europe. The OAG’s investigation alleges that from Jan. 1, 2020, through Aug. 31, 2024, Nasimi, through his practice Tooth Fresh Meadows, located at 61-07 Utopia Pkwy., claimed that he performed hundreds of procedures, including root canals and porcelain crown installations, even though none of them ever happened. As a result, several of his patients were allegedly unable to get the dental treatment they needed because Medicaid records showed that they had already received the procedure that Nasimi billed but never performed. When these patients went to other dentists for procedures, they were denied prior approval for their dental care because Medicaid had already paid Nasimi for those procedures. In July 2022 alone, Nasimi is alleged to have billed for more than $140,000 worth of procedures during periods when his Fresh Meadows practice was closed while he vacationed in England, France, and Greece.   [caption id="attachment_624358" align="alignnone" width="408"] Suleman Nasimi, of Nassau County, through his practice at Tooth Fresh Meadows at 61-07 Utopia Parkway, claimed he performed hundreds of procedures even though none of them happened, according to the charges. Photo via Google Maps[/caption] “Fraudsters who steal from Medicaid with fake billing schemes put vulnerable New Yorkers at risk by making it harder for them to get the care they need,” James said. "All New Yorkers deserve quality dental care, and my office will not tolerate dentists who put personal greed before their patients.” Nasimi and Tooth Fresh Meadows were charged with one count of grand larceny in the second degree, two counts of health care fraud and 35 counts of offering a false instrument for filing in the first degree. Nasimi pleaded not guilty to the charges before Queens Criminal Court Judge Jennifer Saint-Preux, who released him on his own recognizance. If convicted on the top count, Nasimi faces a maximum sentence of five to fifteen years in state prison on the top count. “We will continue to ensure that Medicaid fraudsters are held accountable and criminally prosecuted when they break the law,” James said.

item.dc:creator: Renee DeLorenzo
item.description:

The market will be open every Saturday from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. through Nov. 21, bringing the region’s freshest bounty directly to...
Read More
item.content:encoded:
GrowNYC, an environmental and food access nonprofit, collaborated with the Museum of Modern Art Public School 1 (Moma PS1) to present a seasonal Greenmarket farmers market in Long Island City this fall. The market will be open every Saturday from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. through Nov. 21, bringing the region’s freshest bounty directly to the LIC community.  [caption id="attachment_624334" align="alignnone" width="1200"] Fresh produce offered at one of the Greenmarket farmers markets. Photo courtesy of GrowNYC Greenmarket[/caption] Both Greenmarket and MoMA PS1, two long-standing city institutions, are commemorating their 50th anniversaries — a milestone celebration that inspired the partnership. "We are thrilled to bring a great selection of fresh fruits, vegetables, meats, bread, baked goods and more to the Long Island City community," said Angela Davis, director of GrowNYC Food Access and Agriculture.  “We’re thrilled to be bringing a much-needed Greenmarket to MoMA PS1’s public plaza this fall in partnership with GrowNYC,” added Connie Butler, the Agnes Gund director of MoMA PS1. “As a hub for the community offering free admission for all, visitors will be able to explore our galleries, experience Precious Okoyomon’s living installation in the courtyard, and pick up fresh local foods to take home.” [caption id="attachment_624335" align="alignnone" width="1200"] Guests browse the farmers market. Photo courtesy of GrowNYC Greenmarket[/caption] Participating farmers and producers include:  
  • Halal Pastures, offering certified organic vegetables, certified organic eggs and honey from Orange County, NY.
  • Breezy Hill Orchard, offering orchard fruit, berries, cider and baked goods from Dutchess County, NY.
  • Knead Love Bakery, offering gluten-free breads and baked goods from Kings County, NY. 
  • Wave Hill Bakery, offering breads and baked goods from Fairfield County, CT.
  • Millbrook Beef and Dairy, offering eggs, beef, chicken, pork and cheese from Dutchess County, NY.
  • Mushroom Queens, offering cultivated gourmet mushrooms from Queens County, NY.
[caption id="attachment_624336" align="alignnone" width="1200"] Young guests browse produce. Photo courtesy of GrowNYC Greenmarket[/caption] Since 1976, Greenmarkets have promoted regional agriculture and ensured a continual supply of fresh, local food to the city. GrowNYC operates more than 45 producer-only markets, meaning farms and food makers can only sell products they’ve grown, raised, caught or baked themselves.  All Greenmarket producers come from 250 miles north, 120 miles south and 170 miles east and west of NYC, providing New Yorkers with the fresh, healthy food while helping to preserve farmland in New York’s regional foodshed. [caption id="attachment_624337" align="alignnone" width="1200"] A vendor offers fresh potatoes during a Greenmarket in Jackson Heights. Photo courtesy of GrowNYC Greenmarket[/caption] The Greenmarket program has hosted 46 seasonal and year-round markets that bring fresh produce to NYC neighborhoods. It maintains a network of over 175 farmers and producers, sources food from over 49,000 acres of farmland stewarded and cultivated by farmers and provides over 6,000 unique and heirloom varieties of fruits and vegetables grown by farmers. As part of GrowNYC’s mission to provide equitable access to fresh and local food, all Greenmarket locations accept SNAP EBT, Summer EBT, cash, debit and credit, Healthfirst OTC cards — LIP and CC members only — WIC and Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program (FMNP) coupons, Fresh Connect Checks and Greenmarket Bucks.  Customers using SNAP EBT or Summer EBT that spend $2 receive a bonus $2 Health Buck, up to $10 per day. [caption id="attachment_624338" align="alignnone" width="1200"] More guests visit one of GrowNYC's Greenmarkets. Photo courtesy of GrowNYC Greenmarket[/caption] For more information, follow GrowNYC on Instagram, @grownycgreenmarket, for up-to-date news and special announcements. Guests can also visit individual market webpages for daily farmer attendance and information about upcoming activities such as cooking demonstrations and family-friendly programming. [caption id="attachment_624339" align="alignnone" width="1200"] Martin Rodriguez sells his vegetables at the Corona Farmers Market. Photo courtesy of GrowNYC Greenmarket[/caption]

item.title: Queens among 150 best cities for renters in U.S.: Report
item.dc:creator: By Ethan Marshall
item.description:
Queens was ranked the 147th best place to live for renters in the United States in 2026 in a report from RentCafe. item.content:encoded: Queens was ranked the 147th best place to live for renters in the United States in 2026 in a report from RentCafe. The ranking was based on an analysis of 20 key metrics, which were then grouped into three broad categories: cost of living and housing, local economy and quality of life. Queens ranked 144th in housing and cost of living, which accounts for 40% of the overall score. The cost of living there was 53.8% more than the national average. Its 15.2% share of new apartments was the second-highest of the three New York City boroughs included on the list, ahead of Manhattan's 4% and right behind Brooklyn's 15.6%. The average apartment size of 730 square feet in Queens was the smallest among the boroughs and the third-smallest out of the 150 locations. Queens also had the third-highest occupancy rate nationwide, at 97.8%. The borough ranked much better in the local economy, in 98th place, accounting for 35% of the overall ranking. This is in large part thanks to a 31.4% jump in renter income over the last five years. However, there was just a 0.4% increase in job growth over this period of time. The report also determined that Queens has 148 businesses per 10,000 residents. Queens placed 76th in quality of life, which factored into 25% of the ranking. The borough performed well in the percentage of renters who use public transportation or who walk, at 46.8%, ranking third in the nation. It also had the best school quality ranking among the boroughs included and the 22nd best in the United States, with a score of 5.64. However, 62.1% of renters in Queens experience long solo commutes, which is the third-highest nationally. Additionally, only 9.6% of apartments there are found in top-rated locations.

item.title: Corona man charged in fatal stabbing of Jackson Heights man on Roosevelt Avenue: NYPD
item.dc:creator: Bill Parry
item.description:
A Corona man is being held without bail for allegedly stabbing another man to death on Roosevelt Avenue in Jackson Heights during the early morning of Thursday, Sept. 17. Jose Luis Rodriguez Balda, 38, of 38th Avenue, was arraigned on Sept. 19 in Queens Criminal Court on a complaint charging him with murder in the...
Read More
item.content:encoded: A Corona man is being held without bail for allegedly stabbing another man to death on Roosevelt Avenue in Jackson Heights during the early morning of Thursday, Sept. 17. Jose Luis Rodriguez Balda, 38, of 38th Avenue, was arraigned on Sept. 19 in Queens Criminal Court on a complaint charging him with murder in the second degree and criminal possession of a weapon for killing Angel Marcelo Escalante Gamazo, 48, of Roosevelt Avenue near 76th Street. The two men had a verbal dispute in front of a small business at 76-09 Roosevelt Ave. just after 4 a.m., when the argument turned violent. Rodriguez Balda brandished a knife and plunged it into the victim’s torso, just under the arm, causing damage to his axillary artery, according to the criminal complaint. Police from the 115th Precinct in Jackson Heights responded to a 911 call of a man stabbed at the location, where they found Escalante lying in a pool of blood less than a block west of his home. EMS rushed him to Elmhurst Hospital, where he was listed in critical condition. Escalante succumbed to his injuries and was pronounced dead on Friday, Sept. 18. Homicide detectives from the 115th Precinct arrested Rodriguez hours later after interviewing witnesses and reviewing video surveillance from the crime scene, as well as admissions made by the defendant. Rodriguez Balda was arraigned a day later before Queens Criminal Court Judge Lana Schlesinger, who remanded him into custody without bail.
